theme.name: Taxpayer subsidy of licensing costs
theme.claim: Government and police firearms licences are free or priced far below cost (museum and club fees unreviewed since 1995, prohibited weapons licences uncharged for lack of a power), leaving taxpayers to bear roughly £700,000 a year.

text.line: This is to ensure that firearms are only possessed subject to stringent controls and the highest standards of public safety are maintained.
Licences are issued free of charge, or, in the case of museums and shooting clubs, for a fee well below the cost of providing the service.
Currently, the cost to the taxpayer of firearms licences administered by the Government is estimated at around £700,000 per year.

The Home Office and Scottish Government administer these licences to provide an extra level of assurance, national consistency in decision-making and national oversight of the licensing regime, to reflect the increased risk associated with prohibited weapons and un-certificated shooters and ensure that the highest standards of public safety are maintained. ** (Reference: 2)
Currently there is no power to charge for prohibited firearms licences and, as a result, the cost of those licences is entirely subsidised by the public.
Museum and shooting club licences are subject to fees that were last reviewed in 1995 and do not cover the cost of the service.
Currently the Home Office and the Scottish Government issue licences for prohibited firearms (under s5 of the Firearms Act 1968) to relevant businesses, such as arms manufacturers, free of charge.
This cost is currently fully subsidised by the taxpayer.
The law as it stands provides no power to charge for prohibited firearms licences and as a result the cost of those licences is entirely subsidised by the public.
Other Government licences are subject to fees, but these were last reviewed in 1995 and no longer cover the cost of the service.
Meanwhile the prohibited firearms licensing service is fully subsidised by the public.
Fees are charged as set out in Figure 1 although these were last reviewed in 1995 and do not cover the full cost of the service.

The Home Office firearms licensing service, including prohibited firearms, museums and shooting clubs, will cost an estimated £596,000 in 2016-17, plus an estimated £69,000 in cost to the police (for their role in carrying out checks on applicants). ** (Reference: 21, 22)
We estimate the respective costs to the Scottish Government and Police Scotland to be an additional 8% each. This creates an overall cost of £712,000. ** (Reference: 23)
The lack of the necessary enabling powers has previously prevented this change being made.

Total cost of Section 5 prohibited firearm, museum and shooting club licensing The total cost to England & Wales is made up of £596,000 in costs to the Home Office, and £69,000 in costs to the police, equalling an estimated £665,000 per annum.
The total cost to Scotland is made up of £42,000 in costs to the Scottish Government, and £5,000 in costs to Police Scotland, equalling an estimated £47,000 per annum.
The total cost to both England & Wales and Scotland is therefore estimated to be £712,000.

references.reference: The Scottish Government issues licences to organisations based in Scotland, although it does so under the same legislation as England and Wales as firearms policy (with the exception of certain air weapons) is a reserved matter.

theme.name: Higher-risk licences need Government administration
theme.claim: Prohibited weapons, museum and shooting club licences are issued centrally by the Home Office and Scottish Government, with thorough checks and police involvement, to give extra assurance and national consistency, and this work is what imposes the cost.

text.line: Introduction The Government administers a range of firearms licences covering: weapons which are prohibited under section 5 of the Firearms Act 1968; museum collections; and approved rifle clubs and muzzle-loading pistol clubs.

The Home Office and Scottish Government administer these licences to provide an extra level of assurance, national consistency in decision-making and national oversight of the licensing regime, to reflect the increased risk associated with prohibited weapons and un-certificated shooters and ensure that the highest standards of public safety are maintained. ** (Reference: 2)
They may be used legitimately by police forces (for example handguns, automatic weapons and CS spray), subject to strict controls about police use of force, and by the military.
The police and military do not require a licence.
However, a range of organisations that supply them need to be licensed to possess prohibited weapons as part of their business.

Such organisations will include manufacturers, dealers, service providers and transport companies (‘carriers’) in the defence and security sector, supplying police or military forces in the UK or abroad.
There are a range of other circumstances where a prohibited weapons licence may be required.

These include private maritime security companies supplying armed protection from piracy to UK ships in the high-risk area, forensic service providers, gunsmiths that carry out deactivation of prohibited weapons or trade in pistols used for humane slaughter, and Olympic pistol shooters.

Applicants are subject to thorough checks by the Home Office or Scottish Government and the police before an authority is issued, including background checks, an assessment of suitability and proof of genuine business need to possess prohibited firearms.
These checks are repeated on renewal, which generally takes place every 3 years.
Museum licences Museums with firearms collections (which may include prohibited weapons) require a Home Office or Scottish Government licence.

Shooting club approvals Shooting clubs need Home Office or Scottish Government approval if they wish to allow members without a personal firearms certificate to shoot using firearms provided by the club.
Providing this licensing service imposes a cost on the Home Office, the Scottish government and the police.
The Home Office and Scottish Government issue licences for higher risk activities, including activities involving prohibited firearms such as handguns, automatic weapons and missiles.
Prohibited firearms are known as ‘section 5’ weapons because they are defined under section 5 of the Firearms Act 1968.

The Home Office and Scottish Government also issue licences to museums with collections of firearms, which may include section 5 weapons, and to shooting clubs to allow members without their own firearms or certificate to shoot with club weapons.
The Scottish Government issues licences to those organisations based in Scotland, although it does so under the same legislation as England and Wales as this aspect of firearms is reserved.

The Home Office and Scottish Government have responsibility for these aspects of firearms licensing in order to provide an extra level of assurance, national consistency in decision making and national oversight of the licensing regime, to reflect the increased risk to public safety associated with prohibited weapons and with groups of unlicensed shooters.
It is a statutory requirement that these licences are granted by the Government, as opposed to the police.
The police undertake significant work to assess applicants for Home Office firearms licences.
The Home Office commissions police checks which may include background checks on named individuals, interviews, site visits and stock checks.
The police therefore incur a cost for the work undertaken on the Home Office’s behalf and currently meet this cost from their own budget.
Police Scotland carry out the same work on behalf of the Scottish Government for licences issued there, again meeting the cost from their own budget.

references.reference: The Scottish Government issues licences to organisations based in Scotland, although it does so under the same legislation as England and Wales as firearms policy (with the exception of certain air weapons) is a reserved matter.

theme.name: Licence holders are identifiable beneficiaries
theme.claim: The licences are held by a defined set of businesses and organisations (dealers, carriers, maritime security firms, museums, clubs), the groups the Government considers should bear the cost, with police and other firearms fees already raised to full cost recovery.

text.line: Background In England, Wales and Scotland the police are responsible for issuing certificates for civilian firearms such as shotguns used by farmers or those used in recreational shooting.
• prohibited weapons licences, authorising trade or possession of non-civilian weapons;
• museum licences, for museums with firearms collections which may include prohibited weapons;
• approved shooting clubs, allowing members without the relevant personal firearms certificate to shoot using club firearms.

However, a range of organisations that supply them need to be licensed to possess prohibited weapons as part of their business.

Such organisations will include manufacturers, dealers, service providers and transport companies (‘carriers’) in the defence and security sector, supplying police or military forces in the UK or abroad.
There are a range of other circumstances where a prohibited weapons licence may be required.

These include private maritime security companies supplying armed protection from piracy to UK ships in the high-risk area, forensic service providers, gunsmiths that carry out deactivation of prohibited weapons or trade in pistols used for humane slaughter, and Olympic pistol shooters.
Police forces issue licences for non-prohibited firearms such as shotguns used by farmers or for recreational shooting.

Companies that may require a prohibited firearms licence include firearms dealers and transport companies (‘carriers’) supplying the police or military with weapons, components and other equipment and services, and maritime security companies that protect UK ships from piracy.
